title: Bank “fraud department” wants you to move money
setup: Caller ID shows your bank's name. The caller sounds calm and professional.

messages.text: This is Summit Bank's fraud team. Someone in Ohio is trying to wire $4,200 out of your checking account right now.
To protect your money, we'll move it to a new secure account. I'll walk you through sending it with your payment app.

options.label: Follow their steps to move your money
options.feedback: The “secure account” belonged to the scammer. Payment-app transfers you authorize are very hard to get back.

options.label: Hang up and call the number on the back of your card
options.feedback: Your real bank will never ask you to move money to protect it. Calling the number you trust confirms your account is fine.

options.label: Ask them to prove it by telling you your balance
options.feedback: Scammers sometimes have stolen account details. Knowing info about you doesn't prove anything.

redFlags: Told to move money to “protect it”
Caller ID can be spoofed to show your bank's name
safestAction: Hang up and call your bank using the number on your card or in its app. No real bank asks you to transfer money for safety.

title: Real card fraud alert
setup: You signed up for fraud alerts with your bank. You didn't buy gas today.

content.body: Summit Bank: Did you attempt a purchase of $86.40 at FUEL STOP #221 with card ending 4417? Reply YES or NO. We will never ask for your PIN, password, or a code by text.

options.label: Call the number on the back of your card
options.feedback: This was a real alert. Calling the number on your card is always safe and gets the card locked fast.

options.label: Reply NO
options.feedback: Real bank alerts use YES/NO replies with no links. Replying NO blocked the card. If anyone calls afterward asking for codes, hang up.

options.label: Ignore it — it's probably a scam
options.feedback: It was real. Because no one stopped it, the thief kept using your card for days.

redFlags: Comes from the short code your bank uses for alerts
Asks only YES or NO — no link, no code, no PIN
Details a specific charge you can check in your app
safestAction: Real alerts never include links or ask for codes. When in doubt, call the number on the back of your card.

title: Stranger sends you money “by mistake”
setup: Your payment app shows $350 from someone you don't know. A minute later, they message you.

messages.text: OMG I sent my rent to the wrong person 😭 can you please send it back? My landlord needs it today

options.label: Be kind and send the $350 back
options.feedback: Their payment came from a stolen card and was reversed. You lost the $350 you “returned.”

options.label: Tell them to cancel it through the payment app's support
options.feedback: If it was a real mistake, the sender can dispute it. You never send your own money back.

options.label: Send it back to a different account they give you
options.feedback: A “different account” is a classic twist. The original payment bounced and your money was gone.

redFlags: Urgent, emotional request to send it back
safestAction: Don't spend or send the money. Contact the payment app's support through the app and let them reverse it.

title: $499 invoice with a “call to cancel” number
setup: An invoice arrives through a payment service you actually use. You don't recognize the charge.

content.subject: Invoice from Secure Shield Antivirus
content.body:
Annual subscription renewal – Secure Shield Total Protection. This amount will be charged within 24 hours.

Seller note: If you did not authorize this purchase, call our billing department immediately at 1-888-555-0156 to cancel and receive a refund.

options.label: Call the number to cancel
options.feedback: The “billing team” got you to install remote-access software for your refund, then moved money out of your account.

options.label: Open the PayWallet app yourself and check for pending charges
options.feedback: The invoice was sent by a scammer through a real service. Unpaid invoices can't charge you. Your real account showed nothing owed.

options.label: Pay it now and dispute it later
options.feedback: Paying a fake invoice sends money straight to the scammer, and disputes aren't guaranteed.

redFlags: Charge for something you never bought
Phone number in the seller note, not official support
Invoices can come from real addresses because scammers use real invoicing tools
safestAction: Never call numbers in an unexpected invoice. Check your account directly in the app, and report the invoice there.

title: Roommate requests pizza money
setup: Last night your roommate paid for pizza and said they'd send you a request for your half.

options.label: Pay the request
options.feedback: Real request from someone you know, matching something you agreed to. That's how payment apps are meant to work.

options.label: Decline and report it as a scam
options.feedback: No harm done, but this one was real. Your roommate is still waiting on that $21.50.

redFlags: Someone you know, on their usual account
Matches a real conversation and a real amount
safestAction: Payment apps are for people you know and trust. Real requests match what you agreed to.

title: QR sticker on a parking meter
setup: You park downtown. The meter has a QR sticker. Your camera shows a link preview.

content.subject: Pay by phone — scan here
content.body: Fast mobile parking payment. No app needed.
content.sender: Sticker slightly crooked, covering part of the meter's printed instructions

options.label: Scan and pay with your card
options.feedback: The sticker covered the real code. The fake site kept your card number and charged it repeatedly.

options.label: Use the city's official parking app or the meter's card slot
options.feedback: Paying through the official app or the meter itself skips whatever a sticker points to.

options.label: Scan it, but only pay if the page looks professional
options.feedback: Fake payment pages look professional on purpose. Looks aren't a safety check.

redFlags: Link preview shows an unfamiliar .info domain
safestAction: Check the link preview before opening any QR code. For parking, use the official city app, website, or the meter's slot.
